qs.q: When examining brain tissue suspected of having diffuse axonal injury, which laboratory technique is best utilized to demonstrate widespread axonal swellings?
o: Masson trichrome staining for fibrous scar
Perls' Prussian blue staining for iron pigment
Routine hematoxylin and eosin staining alone
qs.e: Axonal swellings in diffuse axonal injury are best demonstrated using silver impregnation or immunoperoxidase stains for axonally transported proteins like amyloid precursor protein and alpha-synuclein. Prussian blue is used for hemosiderin in old contusions, not acute axonal damage.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is a traumatic brain injury caused by shearing forces that disrupt axons throughout the brain, leading to widespread neuronal dysfunction. It often presents with rapid loss of consciousness and can cause long‑term cognitive deficits.

sections.p: DAI results from rotational acceleration or deceleration forces that stretch and tear axons, especially at gray‑white matter junctions. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation and MRI findings of punctate hemorrhages in the corpus callosum, brainstem, or subcortical white matter.
b: MRI is more sensitive than CT for detecting micro‑hemorrhages
CT may appear normal early despite severe injury

sections.p: The most used classification divides DAI into three grades based on imaging and clinical severity: Grade I – widespread axonal damage without focal lesions; Grade II – involvement of the corpus callosum; Grade III – brainstem involvement, often with the worst prognosis.
b: Higher grade predicts higher mortality and persistent vegetative state

sections.p: The primary cause is high‑speed motor vehicle collisions, followed by falls from height, assault, and sports injuries. In low‑resource settings, road traffic accidents remain the leading cause.
b: Rotational forces cause shearing of long axons
Associated injuries include skull fracture and epidural hematoma

sections.p: Patients typically lose consciousness within seconds to minutes of impact, may have a brief lucid interval, then progress to coma. Early signs include pupillary asymmetry, motor posturing, and diffuse neurological deficits.
b: Rapid decline in Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a red flag

sections.p: Imaging and monitoring guide diagnosis and management.

t.b: If unavailable, proceed to clinical assessment and consider transfer for MRI
If MRI unavailable, use serial CT and neurological exams
If EEG not available, monitor for clinical seizure activity

sections.p: Complications arise from secondary brain injury and systemic effects.
b: Hypoxia or hypotension worsening neuronal loss
Deep vein thrombosis in immobilized patients

sections.p: Treatment focuses on preventing secondary injury and supporting recovery.
b: Maintain MAP ≥ 80 mmHg to ensure cerebral perfusion
Avoid hyperventilation unless ICP crisis; use osmotic agents (mannitol, hypertonic saline) if ICP rises
Treat seizures with benzodiazepines then levetiracetam; avoid phenytoin in hepatic dysfunction
Provide prophylactic antibiotics only if open skull fracture present

sections.p: Long‑term care includes neuro‑rehabilitation, cognitive therapy, and monitoring for post‑traumatic epilepsy. Prevention emphasizes helmet use, seat‑belt compliance, and road safety education.
b: Screen for depression and PTSD during recovery

sections.p: Conditions that can mimic DAI on presentation or imaging.
b: Contusion injury – focal hemorrhage visible on CT
Subarachnoid hemorrhage – blood in cisterns, often with thunderclap headache

sections.p: Certain findings may appear reassuring despite severe injury.
b: Normal CT early after trauma does not rule out DAI
Mild pupil asymmetry can be early sign of brainstem involvement

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness, GCS ≤ 8, worsening pupil size, signs of raised intracranial pressure, new seizures, or rapid neurological decline

faq.q: Why is MRI preferred over CT for DAI?
faq.a: MRI detects tiny hemorrhages and axonal injury that CT often misses, allowing accurate grading.

faq.q: Can a patient recover fully from DAI?
faq.a: Recovery varies; lower grades may return to baseline, while higher grades often have lasting cognitive or motor deficits.

faq.q: What is the main goal of acute DAI management?
faq.a: Prevent secondary brain injury by maintaining oxygenation, perfusion, and controlling intracranial pressure.

exam: Explain the pathophysiological mechanism behind diffuse axonal injury and how it relates to the clinical presentation.
Describe the imaging findings that differentiate Grade I, II, and III DAI.
List three immediate management steps for a patient with suspected DAI and justify each.
